task: Claude Code Operation: the CLAUDE.md hierarchy
question: A team adopts Claude Code. The lead wants every developer's sessions to follow the convention "run the full test suite before proposing a commit". One developer also personally prefers very terse answers, which colleagues do not want imposed on them. Where should each instruction live?

options.A: Both in the project's CLAUDE.md, so that all of the team's guidance is kept together in one file
options.B: Both in each developer's own user-level CLAUDE.md, copied onto every machine by hand
options.C: The convention in the project's committed CLAUDE.md, the preference at the user level
options.D: Both typed at the start of each session, so every developer controls exactly what applies

rationale: The CLAUDE.md hierarchy separates scopes: guidance for everyone working in the repository belongs in the project-level file committed with the code, and a personal preference belongs at the user level, where it affects only that developer. Putting both in the project file (A) imposes one person's preference on the whole team. Hand-copied user-level files (B) are unversioned and drift between machines. Retyping instructions each session (D) is not persistent and is easily forgotten.
evidence: the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, repository initialization, and settings.json configuration

question: A team repeatedly asks Claude Code to write release notes following a detailed house procedure: group changes by component, link each ticket, and list breaking changes first. The procedure needs no new data or system access, only the same instructions applied the same way each time, and the team wants to reuse it across its projects. Which approach fits best?

options.A: Package the procedure as a Skill that Claude Code applies whenever release notes are needed
options.B: Build an MCP server exposing a release-notes tool for Claude Code and other clients to call
options.C: Write a custom tool in each repository that formats release notes from the commit history
options.D: Rely on the built-in tools alone, since file reading and shell access already cover the procedure

rationale: What needs reusing is a set of instructions and conventions, not code or access to a system, which is what a Skill packages. An MCP server (B) is for a capability several applications must call and that is maintained independently; it adds a service to run for what is only a procedure. A custom tool in every repository (C) duplicates code to do what instructions already do. The built-in tools (D) supply file and shell access but carry none of the house procedure, so results would vary from run to run.
evidence: Reusable instructions and conventions, not code

task: Claude Code Operation: core components (Agents, subagents)
question: Midway through a refactor in Claude Code, a developer needs to know every place a deprecated configuration key is read across a large monorepo. The refactor plan and the decisions taken so far exist only in the current session. Earlier searches like this flooded the session with output, and later answers lost track of the plan. Which approach fits best?

options.A: Start a fresh session for the search and paste the refactor plan back in by hand afterwards
options.B: Switch to a model with a larger context window so the search output and the plan both fit
options.C: Add a line to CLAUDE.md telling Claude Code to keep the refactor plan in mind at all times
options.D: Delegate the search to a subagent so only its summary of findings returns to the session

rationale: A subagent runs the verbose search in its own context and hands back only the findings, so the main session keeps its plan and stays uncluttered. A fresh session (A) discards the plan that exists only in the current session and depends on manual reconstruction. A larger window (B) delays the same dilution at higher cost. A CLAUDE.md reminder (C) does not stop the search output from crowding the plan out of the session.
evidence: subagents also isolate context so a long investigation does not pollute the main thread

question: A developer has spent a long Claude Code session building a payments feature, now finished and committed. They want to start an unrelated documentation cleanup in the same repository, but in a quick test Claude Code kept steering the docs task back toward the payments code. The team's lasting conventions are already in the project's CLAUDE.md. What should the developer do?

options.A: Stay in the session and tell Claude Code to ignore everything that came before the docs task
options.B: Start a new session for the docs task, relying on CLAUDE.md for the lasting conventions
options.C: Add notes about the payments work to CLAUDE.md so that the docs task sees the full history
options.D: Move to a model with a larger context window so that both tasks fit without interfering

rationale: The payments history is stale context for an unrelated task, and the durable conventions already live in CLAUDE.md, so a new session gives the docs task a clean context without losing anything that matters. Asking the model to ignore earlier context (A) leaves it in the window, where it keeps exerting influence. Writing the payments history into CLAUDE.md (C) makes the pollution permanent for every future session. A larger window (D) keeps the irrelevant history in play at higher cost.
evidence: features (session management, built-in and custom slash commands, headless mode, streaming mode, auto-mode)

question:
A support-triage service moved to claude-opus-5-5 with adaptive thinking switched on. Since then it crashes on many calls, as shown by the snippet and traceback below. What change fixes the parsing?
```python
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    thinking={"type": "adaptive"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket_text}],
)
label = json.loads(resp.content[0].text)
# AttributeError: 'ThinkingBlock' object has no attribute 'text'
```
Which change fixes it?

options.A: Read resp.content[1].text, because the thinking block always occupies index 0 of the list.
options.B: Catch the AttributeError, then resend the request until the first block is a text block.
options.C: Pick the block whose type is "text" from resp.content and parse its text field.
options.D: Send thinking={"type": "disabled"} so that the response starts with the text block again.

rationale: With thinking on, content can begin with a thinking block, and under adaptive thinking whether one appears varies per request. Code must iterate the blocks and branch on type (C). Disabling thinking (D) is rejected with a 400 on Opus 5.5, where thinking is always on. Hard-coding index 1 (A) breaks whenever no thinking block is returned. Retrying until the layout changes (B) burns tokens and treats a normal response shape as an error.
evidence: With thinking on, response.content can start with a thinking block, so iterate blocks and branch on type rather than reading content[0].text.

question: Your agent loop calls claude-sonnet-5-5 with three client tools and parallel tool use left at its default. A reviewer lists five stop_reason branches from the loop. Which two are implemented correctly? (Select TWO.)

options.A: end_turn: append a user message that says "continue", so the model finishes whatever it left out.
options.B: tool_use: run every requested tool, then return all of the tool_result blocks together in a single user message.
options.C: max_tokens: treat the turn as complete, because the model reached a natural stopping point on its own.
options.D: pause_turn: answer with an empty tool_result block so that the server-side tool is allowed to finish.
options.E: refusal: read stop_details.category and send the case to a fallback or human review rather than resending it unchanged.

rationale: A tool_use stop means the model wants tools run; with parallel calls, all tool_result blocks go back in one user message (B). A refusal is a policy decision, so the loop should inspect stop_details and route it elsewhere instead of repeating the same request (E). Max_tokens (C) means output was cut off, not finished. End_turn (A) is a finished answer; nudging it wastes tokens. A pause_turn (D) is handled by sending the assistant content back, not by fabricating a tool_result for a server tool.
evidence: tool_use: run the tool and return the result. pause_turn: send the assistant content back to continue. refusal: read stop_details and retry on a fallback model.

options.A: The broad APIError clause comes first and catches rate limits before the specific handler runs; order them most specific first.
options.B: The raise in the first clause should go, since the SDK already retries every APIError subclass without any attempt limit.
options.C: RateLimitError is raised only for 529 overloaded responses, so a 429 arrives as a different class and skips this clause entirely.
options.D: The retry-after header is expressed in milliseconds, so the sleep call has to convert the value to seconds before it waits.

rationale: RateLimitError is a subclass of APIError, so Python matches the earlier broad clause and the specific one is unreachable; catch typed SDK errors most-specific first (A). RateLimitError maps to 429, not 529 (C). The retry-after header is in seconds (D). The SDK retries a bounded number of times (two by default), not endlessly (B).
evidence: Catch the SDK's typed classes rather than string-matching error messages, handling the most specific classes first.

question: Eight workers share one API key during an overnight enrichment run, and the logs show five different failures. Which two handling rules are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.A: On a 401 authentication_error, retry at once with the same key, because credentials are checked again on every call.
options.B: On a 529 overloaded_error, retry with exponential backoff plus random jitter, and stop after a bounded number of attempts.
options.C: On a 413 request_too_large, resend the identical payload after a short delay, since the gateway is most likely congested.
options.D: On a 400 invalid_request_error, retry with exponential backoff, because validation failures usually clear up within a few seconds.
options.E: On a 429 that carries a retry-after header, wait at least that many seconds before retrying so the next attempt does not fail again.

rationale: A 429 is transient and the retry-after header says how long to wait (E). A 529 overload is transient too; backoff with jitter keeps eight workers from retrying in lockstep (B). A 400 (D) means the request itself is invalid and needs fixing. A 413 (C) means the payload exceeds a size limit and will fail identically. A 401 (A) is a credential problem that retrying cannot repair.
evidence: Retry transient failures (rate limits, 5xx) with exponential backoff, honoring retry-after; 400, 401, 403, 404 and 413 are errors in the request or credentials.

question: A contract-analysis batch service asks claude-opus-5-5 for reports of up to 60,000 output tokens and stores the result in a database; no user watches the output. Calls fail after several minutes of silence behind a corporate proxy that drops idle connections. Which change addresses the cause?

options.A: Retry each timed-out call with exponential backoff until one request happens to finish inside the proxy's idle limit.
options.B: Lower max_tokens to 8,000 and ask for a shorter report, so that no request runs long enough for the proxy to react to it.
options.C: Raise the client-side timeout above ten minutes so that the proxy has more time to wait for the complete response to arrive in full.
options.D: Enable streaming and take the final message from the SDK helper, so data keeps flowing on the connection while it generates.

rationale: Large non-streaming requests sit silent while the model generates, and networks may drop idle connections. Streaming keeps bytes moving, and the SDK can assemble the final Message so no incremental UI is needed (D). A longer client timeout (C) does nothing about a proxy that closes the socket. Shrinking max_tokens (B) changes the product requirement. Retries (A) hit the same silent window every time.
evidence: Avoid setting a large max_tokens without using the streaming Messages API; some networks might drop idle connections after a variable period of time.

options.A: Streaming cannot carry tool_use blocks, so the request has to be made without stream to receive valid arguments.
options.B: Tool arguments stream as text_delta events, which already contain complete JSON objects that can be parsed one by one as they come.
options.C: The buffer should be reset on every delta, because each partial_json string is a complete argument object by itself.
options.D: Tool input streams as partial JSON fragments, so parse the buffer only after the block's content_block_stop event.

rationale: For tool_use blocks the deltas are partial JSON strings that only form valid JSON once the block is complete, so accumulate and parse at content_block_stop (D). Arguments arrive as input_json_delta, not text_delta (B). Each fragment is incomplete, so resetting loses data (C). Streaming does support tool_use blocks (A).
evidence: Tool use deltas are partial JSON strings; accumulate them and parse the JSON once you receive a content_block_stop event.

question: A streaming chat endpoint returned HTTP 200 and relayed about 400 tokens of text before the stream ended with an error event of type overloaded_error. No exception was raised and the user saw a half-finished answer. Which two changes make the endpoint handle this correctly? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Handle error events inside the event loop, because a failure after the stream has begun arrives after the 200 status was sent.
options.B: Treat a missing message_stop event as success, since the content blocks that matter were already delivered to the client.
options.C: Rely on the SDK's automatic retries, which re-issue any request whose stream fails after the response headers were received.
options.D: Resume partially received tool_use and thinking blocks from their last delta by replaying the saved fragments to the API.
options.E: Save the text received so far and, after a backoff delay, send a new request that asks the model to continue from it.

rationale: Mid-stream errors come as error events on a connection that already returned 200, so status-code handling never fires and the loop must watch for them (A). Recovery means keeping the completed text and starting a new, continuing request after backoff (E). Automatic retries (C) cover failures before a response starts, not this. Tool-use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered (D). A missing message_stop (B) signals an incomplete message.
evidence: An error can occur after the API returns a 200 response; tool use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered, so resume from the most recent text block.

question: A research assistant uses a server-side web search tool. For one long query the response arrives with stop_reason "pause_turn"; its content holds a server_tool_use block and a search result block but no final text, so the UI shows an empty answer. What should the loop do?

options.A: Add a tool_result block for the server_tool_use id, then send a new request that carries the search results.
options.B: Treat the turn as finished and show the search result block to the user as though it were the final answer.
options.C: Resend the request with that paused content added as-is, so the server can resume its search
options.D: Raise max_tokens and resend the original request unchanged, because the turn paused when it hit the output limit.

rationale: pause_turn means the server-side tool loop paused; sending the assistant content back lets the model continue (C). Showing raw search blocks (B) skips the answer that is still coming. Server tools run on Anthropic infrastructure, so the client never supplies a tool_result for them (A). Output-limit truncation is max_tokens, a different stop reason (D).
evidence: pause_turn: send the assistant content back to continue.

question:
A tool-using agent on claude-opus-5-5 with adaptive thinking works for single calls but fails on the second request of every tool loop. The helper and the error are shown below. What is the fix?
```python
def add_assistant_turn(messages, resp):
    kept = [b for b in resp.content
            if b.type in ("text", "tool_use")]
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": kept})

# 400 invalid_request_error: messages.1.content.0: `thinking` or
# `redacted_thinking` blocks in the latest assistant message
# cannot be modified.
```
What is the fix?

options.A: Remove the signature field from each thinking block before resending, since the signature is what gets rejected.
options.B: Send thinking={"type": "disabled"} on every request in the loop so that no thinking blocks are ever returned.
options.C: Append resp.content as received, keeping the thinking and redacted_thinking blocks in their original order.
options.D: Add thinking to the allowed types in the filter, then shorten its text to a summary so the history stays small.

rationale: During a tool loop the latest assistant turn must be passed back exactly as received, including thinking and redacted_thinking blocks (C). Editing or shortening a block (D) or stripping its signature (A) is itself a modification and gets the same 400. Disabling thinking (B) is rejected on Opus 5.5, where thinking is always on.
evidence: Pass back every thinking and redacted_thinking block from the assistant turn exactly as received; blocks that were edited, reordered or filtered out return a 400.

options.A: Set output_config.format to the same schema, which also constrains the arguments the model passes to the tool call.
options.B: List the allowed enum values in the system prompt and check the arguments in code before calling the downstream API.
options.C: Add tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "create_ticket"} so that the model must fill the schema exactly right.
options.D: Add "strict": true to the tool definition, with additionalProperties false and every property listed in required.

rationale: Strict tool use validates tool inputs against the schema; it needs additionalProperties false and the fields in required (D). output_config.format shapes the final text response, not tool arguments (A). Forced tool_choice is rejected with a 400 on Sonnet 5.5 and does not enforce types anyway (C). A prompt note plus a check (B) can catch bad input but does not guarantee conforming inputs.
evidence: strict: true on the tool definition enforces JSON Schema compliance on tool inputs; output_config.format controls Claude's response format.

question: A shipping-label extractor on claude-opus-5-5 used to end its messages list with an assistant turn containing "{" to force JSON. After migrating, every call returns a 400 stating that the conversation must end with a user message. Output must still be a valid object matching a fixed schema. What replaces the prefill?

options.A: Force a tool call with tool_choice type "any" and a tool whose input schema matches the label fields, then read its input back.
options.B: Move the opening brace into the system prompt and keep a final assistant message so that the model continues from there on after it.
options.C: Ask for JSON in the user message and add a retry loop that resends the request until json.loads accepts the reply it gets.
options.D: Request output_config.format with the label schema and read the validated JSON from the response, for example via messages.parse.

rationale: Prefill returns a 400 on current models; structured outputs through output_config.format replace it and give schema-valid JSON (D). Keeping a final assistant message (B) still hits the same error. Forced tool use (A) is also rejected with a 400 on Opus 5.5. Prompt-and-retry (C) can reach valid syntax but gives no schema guarantee and wastes calls.
evidence: Prefilling assistant messages returns a 400 on newer models; use structured outputs or output_config.format instead.

question: A legal-research tool sends three PDF contracts as document blocks and wants answers with page references. A developer set citations.enabled on the first document only and also set output_config.format to a JSON schema for the answer. The API rejects the request with a 400. Which two changes produce a valid request that still shows page references? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Remove output_config.format, because citations cannot be combined with a JSON output schema in the same request.
options.B: Move citations.enabled to the top level of the request, where it applies to the documents of every message.
options.C: Add a system prompt line asking for page numbers, which the API treats as turning the citations feature on.
options.D: Replace the PDFs with plain-text documents, which accept citations together with a response schema.
options.E: Enable citations on all three document blocks, because the setting cannot be enabled for only some documents in one request.

rationale: Citations must be enabled on all documents or none in a request (E), and citations conflict with output_config.format, which returns a 400 (A). Plain-text documents (D) are subject to the same format conflict. Citations are configured per document block, not at the request top level (B). A prompt instruction (C) does not enable the citations feature or produce structured citation entries.
evidence: Citations must be enabled on all or none of the documents within a request; the API returns a 400 if citations are enabled with output_config.format.

options.A: Prefill an opening text block so that the model skips its reasoning and starts writing the answer immediately instead.
options.B: Set thinking to {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 1000} so that reasoning is capped below the output limit.
options.C: Retry the identical request, since the length of the reasoning varies and a later attempt will probably finish in time.
options.D: Raise max_tokens, which covers thinking plus the answer, and stream the request so the larger limit avoids timeouts.

rationale: Thinking tokens are output tokens and share max_tokens with the visible answer; here reasoning consumed all 2000, leaving no text. The fix is a larger limit, streamed to avoid long-request timeouts (D). Prefill (A) is rejected with a 400 on current models. budget_tokens (B) is removed on current models. Retrying the same request (C) reproduces the truncation whenever the reasoning is similarly long.
evidence: max_tokens serves as a hard limit on total output (thinking plus response text), so set a large max_tokens at higher effort levels.

question: A summarization service moves to claude-opus-5-5 without changing its request, which sets thinking to {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 8000}. Every call now fails with a 400, and the team still wants to control how deeply the model reasons. What is the correct request?

options.A: Set thinking to {"type": "disabled"} and add output_config.effort "low" to hold reasoning cost close to the old level.
options.B: Keep the enabled setting and move the 8000-token allowance into max_tokens, which now decides how long the model reasons.
options.C: Keep thinking enabled, but raise budget_tokens to 16000 so the larger allowance satisfies the model's new minimum.
options.D: Set thinking to {"type": "adaptive"} and choose the depth with output_config.effort, for example "medium" or "high".

rationale: Newer models removed manual extended thinking: enabled with budget_tokens returns a 400, and depth is controlled by adaptive thinking plus output_config.effort (D). A larger budget (C) is still the rejected parameter. Disabling thinking (A) is also a 400 on Opus 5.5, where thinking is always on. max_tokens (B) is only a hard output cap, not a depth control.
evidence: "thinking.type.enabled" is not supported for this model. Use "thinking.type.adaptive" and "output_config.effort" to control thinking behavior.

question: A retail chatbot on claude-haiku-5-5 answers short FAQ questions at thousands of requests per minute. Latency and output cost matter most, and the answers are already accurate. Which request-level change fits?

options.A: Set thinking to {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 1024} to give a small, bounded reasoning allowance.
options.B: Cap max_tokens at about 150 tokens so that responses stop early, whatever the model had planned to say.
options.C: Turn on streaming, which lowers the number of output tokens billed for each response.
options.D: Set output_config.effort to "low" so the model spends fewer tokens on reasoning and elaboration for simple questions.

rationale: Effort is the supported control for trading thoroughness against token use and speed; low suits simple, high-volume requests (D). A tight max_tokens (B) truncates answers mid-sentence instead of making them shorter. budget_tokens (A) is removed on current models. Streaming (C) improves perceived latency only; the token count and the bill are unchanged.
evidence: low: simpler tasks that need the best speed and lowest costs, such as subagents, chat, short tool tasks, and simple, high-volume requests.

question: A catalog service sends the same twelve 6 MB product photos, base64-encoded, with each of roughly 500 requests per hour to answer shopper questions. Payloads are huge and upload time dominates latency. Which change fits?

options.A: Convert the photos to base64 text and place them in the system prompt, where they are sent once per session.
options.B: Add cache_control to the base64 image blocks so the API no longer needs the bytes in the request body of each call.
options.C: Upload each photo once through the Files API and reference it by file_id in an image block on every call.
options.D: Switch to the Message Batches API, so the photos are uploaded once for each batch of shopper questions that is queued.

rationale: The Files API lets you upload once and reference a file_id across requests, removing the repeated payload (C). Batches (D) are asynchronous and unsuited to interactive shoppers. A system prompt (A) is still part of every request. Prompt caching (B) reduces processing cost for the prefix, but the bytes must still be sent each time.
evidence: Upload files once, reference them by file_id in Messages requests.

question: An insurance app sends a 40-page scanned claim PDF plus the adjuster's question to claude-sonnet-5-5. Adjusters usually ask several questions about the same claim, and the charts and stamps on the pages matter. Answers are good, but calls are slow and input cost is high. Which two practices fit? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Run OCR first and send only the extracted text, which keeps the charts and stamps while cutting the page images.
options.B: Add cache_control to the document block, since several questions will be asked about the same claim.
options.C: Send each page in its own request and join the answers, because the model reads a single page per call.
options.D: Set a detail: "low" field on the document block, so the model skips the page images and bills only the text.
options.E: Place the document block ahead of the adjuster's question in the user content, so the question follows the material it refers to.

rationale: Documents work best placed before the text of the request (E), and caching the document makes repeated questions on the same claim cheaper and faster (B). OCR-only input (A) drops the visual content that matters. There is no detail field on document blocks (D). The model reads the whole PDF, text and page images together, so per-page requests (C) lose cross-page context.
evidence: Place PDFs before text in your requests; cache PDFs with prompt caching to improve performance on repeated queries.

question: A team moving a document-QA service to a model with a newer tokenizer wants to know whether its worst-case request (system prompt, 14 tool definitions and a 90-page PDF) still fits the per-request token budget. They want the figure without sending a billable generation request. How should they measure it?

options.A: Count the characters of the prompt, divide by four, and add the tool schemas as a fixed overhead.
options.B: Send the request with max_tokens set to 1 and read usage.input_tokens from the response.
options.C: Call the token counting endpoint with the target model and the complete request, then compare the count against the budget.
options.D: Run an open-source tokenizer such as tiktoken locally and add a constant number of tokens for each PDF page.

rationale: The count_tokens endpoint accepts the same inputs as a message (system, tools, images, PDFs), is free, and uses the target model's tokenizer (C). Character heuristics (A) and third-party tokenizers (D) do not match Claude's tokenizer, which differs between model generations. A max_tokens-1 call (B) is still a billable generation request.
evidence: Token counting is free; it accepts system prompts, tools, images and PDFs. Use the endpoint rather than other tokenizers.

question:
An internal Q&A tool sends a policy PDF with citations enabled and prints the answer, but users never see page references. The call and display code are below. Why are the references missing?
```python
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document", "title": "Travel policy",
         "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf",
                    "data": pdf_b64},
         "citations": {"enabled": True}},
        {"type": "text", "text": question}]}],
)
print("".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text"))
```
Why are the references missing?

options.A: Citations sit on each text block as page_location entries; the code reads only its text.
options.B: Citations are returned in a separate top-level citations list on the response, which this code never reads.
options.C: A base64 PDF is accepted but never yields citation entries, because the source type has to be a URL.
options.D: The cited_text field appears only when the system prompt tells the model to quote its sources.

rationale: Each text block in the response can carry its own citations array; for PDFs the entries are page_location items. The display code joins only b.text and discards b.citations (A). There is no top-level citations field (B). Base64 PDFs support citations (C). Citations come from the citations setting on the document block, not from prompt wording (D).
evidence: Each text block can contain a claim and a list of citations that support it; PDFs use page_location citations.

question:
A support bot gets a 400 on the request that follows a tool call, with the message "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after: toolu_01A". The messages it sent are below. What must change?
```json
[
  {"role": "user", "content": "Where is order 8841?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Checking."},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01A", "name": "get_order",
     "input": {"id": "8841"}}]},
  {"role": "user", "content": "Please hurry."}
]
```
What must change?

options.A: Place the tool_result in a new assistant message, so that the roles alternate correctly after the tool_use.
options.B: Insert a system-role message between the assistant turn and the last user turn to carry the order lookup.
options.C: Begin the final user message with a tool_result block whose tool_use_id is toolu_01A, and put any text after it.
options.D: Remove the text block from the assistant turn, because a tool_use block must be the only content of its message at all.

rationale: Every tool_use must be answered by a tool_result with the matching id in the very next user message, ahead of any other content (C). Messages have only user and assistant roles; system goes in the top-level parameter (B). Text and tool_use can share an assistant turn (D). Tool results belong to the user role, never the assistant (A).
evidence: Tool results go in the user message that immediately follows the tool_use, with tool_result blocks first in the content (paraphrase).

question: A QA tool sends a "before" and an "after" screenshot of a checkout page in one request, with the instruction "What changed in the second one compared with the first?". Answers often mix the two images up. Which change most directly fixes this?

options.A: Move the images into the system prompt, where the model gives them stronger priority than user content.
options.B: Merge both screenshots into one side-by-side image, so that the model reads them as a single picture.
options.C: Send each screenshot in a separate request and ask the model to compare its two answers afterwards.
options.D: Put a short text block such as "Image 1:" before each image block, and refer to those labels in the question.

rationale: With several images, introduce each with a short text label and refer to the labels in the prompt (D). Merging into one picture (B) removes the clean per-image reference and wastes resolution. Separate requests (C) lose the direct comparison. Image blocks belong in user content; the system prompt (A) does not give them any higher priority.
evidence: Introduce each image with a short text label (Image 1:, Image 2:) so you can refer to them by name in your prompt and in follow-up turns.

question: A team uploaded a 250-page product manual through the Files API and asks about 30 questions per hour against it from claude-sonnet-5-5 using the file_id. They expected uploads to remove the document from the bill, but input cost stays high on every call. What explains this, and what reduces it?

options.A: A file_id reference is billed as input only on the first request in a workspace, so the repeat charges must come from output tokens.
options.B: Referenced files are charged at the output token rate, so converting the PDF to text before uploading avoids the higher price.
options.C: The file's content is billed as input tokens on each request that references it; add cache_control to the document block to reuse it cheaply.
options.D: Each file_id lookup is charged as a Files API operation, so batching the thirty hourly questions into one request removes that fee.

rationale: Files API operations are free, but file content used in a Messages request is priced as input tokens each time. Prompt caching on the document block lowers repeat cost (C). There is no per-lookup fee (D), the content is billed on every request (A), and file content is not billed at the output rate (B).
evidence: Files API operations are free; file content used in Messages requests is priced as input tokens.

question: A support-tooling team turns two business requirements into a design: agents must see the first words of an AI-drafted reply within about two seconds, and traffic peaks near 4,500 requests per minute at 9 a.m. against a 4,000 RPM limit on the chosen model. Which two derived requirements address them? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Send the drafts through the Message Batches API to halve cost and lift throughput
options.B: Stream the draft so the first tokens reach the agent's screen while generation continues
options.C: Set max_tokens higher so that long drafts are not cut off during the 9 a.m. spike
options.D: Request a higher RPM limit and queue overflow client-side, backing off per the retry-after header
options.E: Turn off SDK retries so a failed draft shows an error to the agent immediately

rationale: The two-second target is about time to first token, which streaming addresses (B). The peak exceeds the RPM limit, so capacity must be raised and the overflow absorbed by a queue that honors retry-after (D). Batches (A) are asynchronous with up to 24 hours of latency, so they cannot serve live agents. A higher max_tokens (C) changes truncation, not latency or throughput. Disabling retries (E) turns every 429 into a visible failure.
evidence: Streaming improves perceived latency (time to first token); a 429 carries retry-after; Message Batches complete within 24 hours and are not for interactive traffic.

question: A clinic's compliance officer requires an audit trail for every AI-generated patient summary: what the model was shown, which model and prompt produced the output, retained for seven years, with no patient data placed in outside tools. Which derived requirement meets all of this?

options.A: Depend on the API provider's own log retention to reproduce transcripts whenever an auditor asks about a specific patient summary
options.B: Forward each request and response to a hosted tracing service that offers full-text search across every stored trace and prompt version
options.C: Persist request ID, model ID, prompt version, and full input and output in the clinic's encrypted store with seven-year retention
options.D: Keep the clinician-approved final summary with a timestamp and the clinician's ID in the records table, as with other notes

rationale: The audit requirement implies capturing inputs, outputs, and the exact model and prompt version, in storage the clinic controls and retains for seven years (C). Provider-side retention (A) is neither under the clinic's control nor guaranteed for seven years. A third-party tracing service (B) violates the no-outside-tools constraint. Storing only the approved summary (D) loses what the model saw and which versions produced it.
evidence: Derive requirements from the audit and privacy constraints: log request ID, model, prompt version, full I/O in your own controlled store.

question: A claims-triage service pins claude-sonnet-4-6 in production. The team wants to move to claude-sonnet-5-5, and the offline regression suite shows the same accuracy on both. Latency, output length, and token counts have not been compared on live traffic. What should happen before the move reaches 100% of traffic?

options.A: Switch every request to the new ID now, because matching offline accuracy on the regression suite already shows the two models are interchangeable
options.B: Run both models on every request indefinitely, comparing their answers and keeping whichever one is cheaper to produce each time
options.C: Send a small canary slice to the new pinned ID, compare live cost, latency, and parse failures per version, with the old ID ready for rollback
options.D: Hold the old model until its retirement notice arrives, then migrate all traffic in a single scheduled release

rationale: A staged rollout verifies what the offline suite cannot: live cost per request, latency, stop reasons, and parse failures per model version, with the previous pinned ID kept ready for rollback (C). Cutting over on offline accuracy alone (A) skips the production signals. Running both models on every request (B) doubles cost and is an over-engineered cascade. Waiting for a retirement deadline (D) concentrates all risk into a rushed release.
evidence: Pin model IDs in production; re-run evals before switching; canary releases limit blast radius and make rollback a configuration change.

question:
A prompt change (v14) is in a 5% canary next to the current prompt (v13). The release pipeline posts this comparison after 30 minutes:

```text
window=30m   canary=5%   model=claude-sonnet-5-5 (both)
metric                   v13 (95%)   v14 (5%)
requests                   5,410       287
json_parse_errors           0.3%       8.4%
stop_reason=max_tokens      0.2%       9.1%
avg output_tokens            412      1,046
p95 latency                 3.1 s      7.8 s
```

What should the release process do?

options.A: Promote v14 to 100%, since more than 90% of canary requests parsed successfully and the pipeline can absorb the rest
options.B: Halt promotion, roll back to v13, then shorten v14's outputs and re-run the evals before another canary
options.C: Keep v14 at 5% and add an automatic retry on JSON parse failure, which hides the truncation at no extra cost to users
options.D: Raise max_tokens for v14 and then promote it, since truncation is the only meaningful difference between the versions

rationale: The max_tokens stop reasons (9.1%) line up with the parse errors (8.4%): v14 makes outputs far longer (about 2.5x tokens and latency), so JSON is cut off. The pipeline should stop and revert by switching the prompt pointer back to v13, then fix and re-evaluate (B). A 90% parse rate (A) is a large regression from 99.7%. Retrying (C) repeats the same long generation, doubling cost and latency. Raising max_tokens (D) ignores that output length, cost, and latency also changed.
evidence: Compare canary metrics per version against the baseline; roll back by switching the config pointer; stop_reason max_tokens means the output was truncated.

question: Three teams edit prompt strings that live inside Python files. After a bad answer reaches a customer, nobody can say which prompt text produced it, because several edits shipped the same week. What change fixes the traceability problem?

options.A: Add a dated comment above each prompt string and ask every editor to bump it whenever they change the wording
options.B: Version each prompt as an artifact with an ID or hash, select it through config, and log it on every request
options.C: Rely on the repository's commit history to reconstruct which prompt text was active at the time of the incident
options.D: Move the prompts into an admin page that anyone on the three teams can edit, so changes happen quickly

rationale: Traceability needs the version to be explicit in config and recorded with each request, so any output can be tied to the exact prompt text (B). Comments (A) depend on discipline and can drift from reality. Commit history (C) shows what was written, not which version was live for a given request. An open edit page (D) adds more unreviewed changes and no record.
evidence: Treat prompts as versioned artifacts; pin the version in configuration and record it alongside each request so evals and incidents can be reproduced.

question:
This file is committed to the repository and deployed unchanged to production:

```yaml
# config/production.yaml
anthropic:
  model: claude-sonnet-5-5
  prompt: prompts/triage@latest
  max_tokens: 1024
  api_key: sk-ant-api03-Zk3FakeKeyForExample
```

Which two changes bring it in line with sound configuration management? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Replace the model ID with a floating alias so the service adopts each new model release automatically
options.B: Pin the prompt to a specific version or hash instead of @latest, so deploys run only an evaluated prompt
options.C: Base64-encode the key value so that it is no longer readable at a glance by people browsing the repository
options.D: Keep only a secret reference here; the service reads the key from a secrets manager at runtime
options.E: Move the model line into application code so that it can never differ between the environments

rationale: An unpinned @latest prompt means any edit reaches production without passing the eval gate, so the version must be fixed (B). A key in a committed file is exposed to everyone with repository access and its history, so the file should hold only a reference to a secrets manager (D). A floating alias (A) undermines the model pin the file already has. Base64 (C) is encoding, not protection. Hard-coding the model in code (E) removes environment-specific configuration instead of managing it.
evidence: Pin model and prompt versions in production; keep API keys out of code and config files, in a secrets manager or environment.

question: A 3,000 requests-per-minute load test in staging made production chat start returning 429 errors, though production traffic had not changed. Both environments use keys from the same workspace on claude-sonnet-5-5. The team wants a guarantee that testing can never consume production headroom. What should they do?

options.A: Move staging to its own workspace and key, with a workspace rate limit set below the organization's limit so tests cannot take production's headroom
options.B: Raise the SDK's max_retries in production so that rejected chat requests are tried again until they succeed
options.C: Run staging load tests against claude-haiku-5-5 so the test draws on a different model's limit bucket
options.D: Request a higher usage tier so that staging and production traffic together fit under the same pooled limit

rationale: Rate limits are enforced at the organization level and shared across workspaces unless limits are set per workspace; a dedicated staging workspace with its own lower limit caps what tests can take (A). More retries (B) add load to an exhausted bucket. Testing another model (C) no longer validates the production configuration and does not isolate environments. A higher tier (D) adds capacity but not a guarantee, because the shared pool can still be consumed.
evidence: You can set custom spend and rate limits for each workspace; organization-wide limits always apply.

options.A: The 5-minute TTL expired between the calls, so the entry should be written with a 1-hour TTL to survive the gap between requests
options.B: The manual is shorter than the minimum cacheable length, so it must be padded before it can be cached
options.C: Only one breakpoint is set, so a second cache_control marker should be added on the user message
options.D: The changing timestamp at the start alters the prefix on each call; move it out of the cached block, after the breakpoint

rationale: Caching matches an identical prefix up to the breakpoint. A timestamp at the front makes every call write a new entry (cache_creation is non-zero each time, cache_read stays 0), so the volatile text belongs after the breakpoint, such as in the user message (D). Twenty seconds is well inside the 5-minute TTL (A). A prompt below the minimum would show 0 for both counters (B). A second breakpoint (C) cannot make a changing prefix match.
evidence: Cache hits require 100 percent identical prompt segments up to the cache_control block; both counters 0 means the prompt was not cached.

question: A university registrar's assistant prepends a 24,000-token course catalog to each request. Every six hours an announcement triggers about 300 student queries within four minutes; between bursts there is almost no traffic. The catalog is cached with a breakpoint after it. Which TTL setting is best?

options.A: The 1-hour TTL, so that the entry survives the quiet period between bursts and the first query of each burst is a hit
options.B: Skip caching, because traffic this bursty cannot produce enough cache reads to ever repay the extra cost of the cache write
options.C: The default 5-minute TTL; each read refreshes the entry during the burst, and a 1-hour TTL only adds write cost
options.D: The default TTL plus a keep-alive request every four minutes between bursts to hold the entry warm until the next one

rationale: Within a four-minute burst each read refreshes the 5-minute entry, so hundreds of queries pay the cheap read price and only the first pays the write (C). The 1-hour TTL (A) pays a higher write multiplier but still expires long before the next burst six hours later, so every burst starts with a write anyway. Skipping caching (B) forgoes about 300 cheap reads per burst. Keep-alive pings (D) pay for requests that serve no user.
evidence: The cache is refreshed at no extra cost each time the cached content is used; the 1-hour TTL costs 2x the base input price to write.

question: A contract-review assistant sends, in this order: 14 tool definitions, a 3,500-token system prompt, a 30,000-token contract specific to each session, the running conversation, and a per-request "current time" line. Thousands of sessions run in parallel, each with many turns. Which two design choices maximize cache reuse? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Place the contract before the system prompt so that the largest block is the earliest part of the prefix
options.B: Put a breakpoint after the system prompt so the tools and instructions are shared by every session
options.C: Put the current-time line at the top of the system prompt so the model always sees it first
options.D: Mark each conversation turn with its own breakpoint so every earlier turn is cached separately
options.E: Put a second breakpoint after the contract so later turns of the same session read it from cache

rationale: The prefix order is tools, system, then messages. A breakpoint after the system prompt lets all sessions share the tools and instructions (B), and a second one after the contract lets each session reuse its own 30,000 tokens on later turns (E); the time line should sit in the final message after the last breakpoint. Putting the contract first (A) makes the prefix differ per session, so nothing is shared. A timestamp at the top (C) invalidates everything after it. A breakpoint on every turn (D) exceeds the limit of four.
evidence: Prefixes are created in the order tools, system, messages; up to 4 breakpoints; put volatile content after the last breakpoint.

question: An interactive tutoring chat on claude-sonnet-5-5 keeps hitting its input-tokens-per-minute limit with 429 errors. Roughly 85% of each request is the same 30,000-token course pack, resent uncached on every turn. The team wants more effective throughput without leaving real-time chat. Which change helps most?

options.A: Move half of the chat turns to the Message Batches API, which has its own separate limits and a lower price
options.B: Lower max_tokens on each request so that the per-request estimate counts less against the input-token limit
options.C: Cache the course pack behind a breakpoint, since cache reads do not count toward the input limit on most models
options.D: Create several keys in the same workspace and rotate requests across them to spread the load evenly

rationale: For most Claude models only uncached input tokens (input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens) count toward ITPM, so reading the course pack from cache raises effective throughput without a limit change (C). Batches (A) return results asynchronously, which breaks live chat. max_tokens (B) is not part of the input-token limit, and output limits count actual tokens only. Limits are applied per organization and workspace, not per key (D).
evidence: cache_read_input_tokens do not count toward ITPM for most models; limits apply at the organization (and workspace) level.

question: An analytics team has four Claude workloads on claude-haiku-5-5. Which one is the best fit for the Message Batches API?

options.A: A checkout flow that scores each cart for fraud and must answer before the payment page finishes loading
options.B: A support copilot that drafts a reply while the agent waits on the open ticket, then lets the agent edit it
options.C: A multi-step research agent in which each call needs the previous call's output to decide the next step
options.D: A quarterly job that re-scores 400,000 archived transcripts for a quality report due in five days

rationale: The Batches API gives 50% lower cost for asynchronous work that can finish within 24 hours, with independent requests and no one waiting (D). The fraud check (A) and the support copilot (B) are latency-sensitive. The research agent (C) has dependent steps, so each request needs the previous result and cannot be submitted up front.
evidence: Message Batches API: asynchronous, 50 percent cost reduction, most batches finish in under an hour, up to 24 hours.

question:
A nightly job submits one batch request per document, then pairs results with documents like this. Occasionally a summary is saved under the wrong document, and a few documents get nothing:

```python
results = list(client.messages.batches.results(batch_id))
for doc, res in zip(docs, results):
    text = res.result.message.content[0].text
    save_summary(doc.id, text)
```

What is the correct fix?

options.A: Sort the results by message ID before zipping them with the documents in the order they were submitted
options.B: Set custom_id to the document ID, then index results by custom_id and branch on result.type
options.C: Submit one request per batch so there is only a single result and ordering can never differ
options.D: Assert that len(results) equals len(docs) before zipping, and abort the job whenever the counts differ

rationale: Batch results can arrive in any order, so position says nothing about which document a result belongs to; the custom_id echoed in each result does. Results may also be errored, canceled, or expired and then have no message to read (B). Message IDs (A) are unrelated to submission order. One request per batch (C) defeats the purpose and still needs handling of failures. A length check (D) can pass while the pairing is still wrong.
evidence: Use meaningful custom_id values to match results with requests, because order is not guaranteed; results have types succeeded, errored, canceled, expired.

options.A: Resubmit the whole batch so that all 50,000 results come from a single consistent run
options.B: Collect the custom_ids of expired and api_error entries and resubmit them as-is in a new batch
options.C: Resubmit the invalid_request_error entries unchanged, since the failure was probably transient
options.D: Inspect and correct the request bodies behind invalid_request_error entries before resubmitting them
options.E: Cancel the batch so that the errored requests are released and processed again automatically

rationale: Server-side errors and expired requests were not processed or billed, so resubmitting just those custom_ids is safe (B). An invalid_request_error means the body itself is wrong, so it must be fixed first (D). Rerunning everything (A) pays again for the 48,812 successes. Unchanged invalid requests (C) will fail again. The batch has already ended, so cancel (E) does nothing and never reprocesses requests.
evidence: errored/expired requests are not billed; invalid_request_error must be fixed before re-sending, server errors can be retried directly.

question: A company chooses Claude through its AWS Bedrock account for IAM integration and consolidated billing. The design leans on a feature announced last month in the first-party API documentation. Before committing the architecture, what should the team do?

options.A: Assume parity, since the same model is served and a model ID mapping is all that differs
options.B: Move the whole workload to the first-party API, because third-party platforms never get new features
options.C: Check the platform-specific documentation for that feature's availability and plan a supported fallback if it is missing
options.D: Ship on Bedrock and wait for runtime errors in staging to show which features are unsupported

rationale: Cloud-provider platforms can lag or differ from the first-party API in features, beta access, and lifecycle dates, so availability must be verified per platform before design, with a fallback for gaps (C). Same model does not mean same feature set (A). Platforms do receive features, just not always simultaneously, so the blanket claim (B) is false and discards the IAM and billing reasons for the choice. Discovering gaps through runtime errors (D) turns a design question into a late failure.
evidence: Features and availability may differ between partner-operated platforms and the direct API.

question: Developers run an application against the first-party API on laptops, while production runs on Bedrock for IAM reasons. The model identifier strings and client setup differ between the two, and a hard-coded production string just broke a developer's local run. How should the application handle this?

options.A: Derive the Bedrock inference profile ID at runtime by applying a regex to the first-party model name
options.B: Point developers at the production Bedrock account so that every environment uses an identical model string
options.C: Hard-code both identifiers in application code and select one with an if-statement on the hostname at startup
options.D: Make the provider, client settings, and exact pinned model identifier environment-specific config, loaded at startup

rationale: Provider choice, credentials, and pinned model identifier are deployment details and belong in environment-specific configuration, so each environment states exactly what it calls (D). Regex derivation (A) is brittle because identifier formats are set by each platform. Developer access to the production account (B) breaks least privilege and costs money. Hostname branching in code (C) spreads configuration through the codebase.
evidence: On Bedrock the model is addressed by an inference profile ID or ARN rather than the first-party model name; lifecycle dates differ by platform.

question:
On the 12th of the month a service starts failing. The SDK retries three times with backoff, then raises. Logs show:

```text
HTTP 429  attempts=3/3  request-id=req_018EeWyXxfu5pfWkrYcMdjWG
retry-after: (absent)
{"type":"error","error":{"type":"rate_limit_error",
 "message":"You have reached your API usage limits ... You will regain access on 2026-12-01 at 00:00 UTC.",
 "details":{"error_code":"enforced_spend_limit_reached"}}}
```

What is the right response?

options.A: Raise max_retries and add jitter, because rate-limit errors clear once the backoff delay is long enough
options.B: Cut concurrency so that the service stays under its requests-per-minute limit from this point on
options.C: Rotate to a second API key in the same organization, which carries its own separate limit
options.D: Stop retrying on this code, alert on-call, then request a higher tier or wait for the reset time

rationale: The error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached with no retry-after means the monthly spend cap has been hit, not a per-minute limit; access stays blocked until the reset or a tier increase, so retries cannot succeed. Detect it, alert, and raise the cap (D). More backoff (A) cannot clear it. Lower concurrency (B) addresses RPM, which was not exceeded. Spend caps are organization-wide, so another key (C) shares the same cap.
evidence: Spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header; error.details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached; retrying fails until access resumes.

question: A hotel chain's product owner writes: "The booking assistant must never quote a rate that is no longer available." Room rates change every few minutes in the inventory system. Which derived functional requirement best captures this?

options.A: Add the nightly rate export to the cached system prompt and tell the assistant to quote only from that export
options.B: Give the assistant a live inventory lookup tool and quote only returned rates, with their timestamp
options.C: Instruct the assistant in the system prompt to avoid quoting any rate it is not completely sure about now
options.D: Use the most capable model tier at high effort so it reasons more carefully about which rates to quote

rationale: A freshness guarantee has to come from the data path: look up the rate at answer time through a tool and restrict quotes to what the tool returned (B). A nightly export in the prompt (A) is stale within minutes. The model cannot know what is no longer available, so an instruction to be sure (C) gives no control. A stronger model (D) still has no access to current inventory.
evidence: Requirements for fresh external data are met with tools that retrieve it at request time, not with model capability or static prompt content.

question: A team's eval set has 12 hand-written happy-path prompts. Last month three production failures slipped through: a hallucinated refund policy, a Spanish-language ticket, and a 40-page email thread that overflowed context. How should the team rebuild the set?

options.A: Have Claude generate 500 synthetic prompts that closely resemble the 12 current ones, to widen the coverage
options.B: Keep the 12 prompts and tune the prompt until every one passes, since a clean pass is the release bar
options.C: Sample anonymized production traffic by category and add each past failure as a permanent case with its expected behavior
options.D: Write 100 more happy-path variants by hand, because failures are rare and cases should reflect the common case

rationale: A useful eval set mirrors real traffic and its edge cases and grows with every escaped failure, so the same bug is caught next time (C). Synthetic near-copies (A) extend only the distribution the team already imagined. Tuning until 12 prompts pass (B) overfits a tiny set. More happy-path variants (D) add volume but not the hard cases that actually failed.
evidence: Build a representative eval set (including edge cases and past failures) before changing prompts or models.

question: An email-reply pipeline must be scored on two things: whether the extracted invoice total, due date, and currency exactly match the source, and whether the apology paragraph sounds appropriately empathetic. Which two grading approaches should the team use? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Use an LLM judge for the extracted fields too, since one grading method is simpler to operate
options.B: Grade the extracted fields with exact-match code against the labeled values, which is fast and deterministic
options.C: Score empathy by counting apology words with a regular expression, as a proxy that never varies
options.D: Grade tone with an LLM judge using a written rubric, checking its scores against a human-labeled sample first
options.E: Ask the model that wrote the reply to rate it 1 to 10 without a rubric, and trust agreement across reruns

rationale: Fields with a single correct value call for a code-based exact-match grader (B). Subjective quality such as tone needs a rubric-driven LLM judge, validated against human labels before it is trusted (D). An LLM judge for exact fields (A) adds cost and nondeterminism where code is exact. Counting apology words (C) measures a keyword, not empathy. A rubric-less self-rating (E) is biased, and consistency between reruns is not accuracy.
evidence: Code-based graders for exact checks, LLM-as-judge with a rubric for open-ended quality (calibrate against human labels).

question:
A release checklist says "ship the candidate model if overall accuracy is at least the baseline's." A regression run on a 410-case support suite produced:

```text
category        cases  baseline  candidate
refunds           120      96%       99%
multilingual       60      88%       71%
long_threads       50      90%       91%
other             180      95%       99%
overall           410    93.7%      93.9%
```

What should the team conclude?

options.A: Ship, because overall accuracy improved and 60 cases are too few to treat the multilingual drop as a real regression in practice
options.B: Ship now and add more multilingual cases to the suite after launch, since customers will report real problems
options.C: Block the release and gate on per-category thresholds, since the overall figure masks a 17-point multilingual regression
options.D: Re-run the suite repeatedly until the candidate's overall score rises clearly above the baseline

rationale: The overall average is hidden by gains elsewhere: multilingual fell from 88% to 71%, a large drop even on 60 cases. Regression gates should check slices and critical categories as well as the mean (C). Calling it noise (A) dismisses a 17-point shift. Shipping and adding tests later (B) uses customers as the eval. Re-running until the average rises (D) is cherry-picking and leaves the regression in place.
evidence: Regression-run on every prompt or model change; compare per-category results, not only one aggregate.

question:
Tickets are landing in the default queue with category=None. An engineer pulls this trace for one of them:

```text
POST /v1/messages  model=claude-sonnet-5-5  max_tokens=24  -> 200
  stop_reason=max_tokens  output_tokens=24
  text='{"category":"billing","priority":"high","summary":"Customer reports a double charge on inv'
parser: JSONDecodeError: Unterminated string starting at char 50
router: category=None -> default queue
```

Where does the failure originate, and what should the engineer do first?

options.A: Model output: it produced malformed JSON, so add more few-shot examples showing correctly terminated JSON
options.B: Model output: the request needs a stricter instruction stating that the reply must be valid JSON only
options.C: Model capability: switch to a larger model tier so that its JSON is better formed overall
options.D: Integration: output was cut at max_tokens; check stop_reason before parsing and raise the limit

rationale: stop_reason=max_tokens with output_tokens equal to the 24-token cap shows the reply was cut off mid-string; what the model wrote was valid so far, and the break is in the integration layer's max_tokens setting and unchecked stop_reason (D). Few-shot examples (A), a stricter JSON instruction (B), and a bigger model (C) all target the model's output, which was not malformed, and would not change the cut-off.
evidence: Always check stop_reason; max_tokens means the output was truncated. Separate integration failures from model-output failures when debugging.

question: An internal assistant passed its launch eval. Three weeks later the retrieval corpus was reorganized and users report worse answers, yet uptime, error-rate, and latency dashboards are green. Which two additions best detect quality drift in production? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Re-run the frozen launch eval nightly and treat a stable score as proof that production quality is unchanged for users
options.B: Score a regular sample of production traces with code checks and a calibrated judge, trended by category
options.C: Alert whenever the share of HTTP 200 responses falls below the service's current availability target level
options.D: Track thumbs-down and regenerations, and send flagged conversations to review and into the eval set
options.E: Report the daily mean of output tokens per response and investigate whenever that number moves noticeably

rationale: Quality drift shows up in what real users send and receive, so sampled production traces need ongoing scoring with graders validated against human labels (B), and user feedback signals must flow to review and become new eval cases (D). A frozen eval (A) cannot reveal changes in live inputs or the corpus. HTTP 200 rates (C) and token counts (E) are operational metrics that can look healthy while answers get worse.
evidence: Monitor production quality with sampled graded traces and feedback loops; failures become new eval cases.

question: A support platform routes 400,000 incoming tickets per day into one of three queues. The product needs a p95 latency under 800 ms and the label set is fixed. On a 2,000-ticket eval drawn from last quarter's traffic, Haiku scored 97.1%, Sonnet 97.4%, and the acceptance bar is 96%. Which deployment fits these constraints?

options.A: Sonnet, because the 0.3-point lead on the eval will compound across 400,000 daily tickets
options.B: Opus at low effort, because the strongest tier at reduced effort can match smaller models on latency
options.C: Sonnet with a cached system prompt, so its latency and cost come close to the smaller tier
options.D: Haiku, because it clears the 96% bar and is the fastest, cheapest tier for high-volume labeling

rationale: Haiku meets the measured quality bar and is the tier built for high-volume, latency-sensitive, simple tasks, so it is the cheapest option that satisfies every constraint. (A) pays for margin the acceptance bar does not require; a 0.3-point gap is also within eval noise. (B) Opus at any effort is still a larger, slower, costlier model than the task needs. (C) caching lowers input cost but does not change per-token generation speed or the tier price, so it does not match Haiku.
evidence: Pick the cheapest tier that meets the quality bar measured by an eval; Haiku suits high-volume, latency-sensitive, simple tasks.

question: A code-review service sends every pull request to Haiku first and escalates to Opus when Haiku reports low confidence. About 35% of PRs escalate, so those pay for two calls, and cache hit rates are poor because each tier keeps its own cache. Engineers want a simpler design with similar review quality. What should the team evaluate?

options.A: Add a Sonnet middle stage so fewer PRs reach Opus, keeping the cascade but cutting the escalation rate of expensive calls
options.B: Cache the Haiku output and feed it to Opus as context so the second call is cheaper on every escalated PR
options.C: Run every PR on Opus at a lower effort setting and compare quality, latency, and cost against the cascade
options.D: Raise the escalation confidence threshold so that fewer than 10% of PRs ever reach the Opus tier

rationale: The stronger model at lower effort is a single-model alternative: one cache, one call per PR, and effort trims thinking cost, so it should be measured before keeping a multi-model cascade. (A) adds yet another model-scoped cache and more calls. (B) caches are model-scoped and Haiku output is not a reusable prefix for Opus. (D) tuning the threshold only trades review quality for cost without removing the double-call or cache problems.
evidence: Try the stronger model at lower effort before building multi-model cascades (caches are model-scoped).

question: After enabling adaptive thinking at high effort on Sonnet for a contract-summary feature, the monthly bill roughly doubled while the visible summaries stayed the same length and request volume was unchanged. Usage logs show output_tokens per request rose sharply but input_tokens did not move. Where is the extra spend most likely coming from?

options.A: Thinking blocks are stored server-side and billed as cache writes at the premium rate until the response expires
options.B: Adaptive thinking re-sends the full conversation history on each internal step, which inflates input_tokens on the invoice
options.C: The higher effort setting selects a more expensive per-token price tier for every token generated in the response
options.D: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, so deeper reasoning inflates output_tokens even when the visible text is unchanged

rationale: Thinking is billed as output tokens, and output costs several times input per token, so a higher effort level can raise spend with no change in the visible answer. Lowering effort for easy requests is the lever. (B) input_tokens did not move in the logs. (C) effort changes how many tokens are generated, not the per-token price. (A) thinking is not billed as cache writes.
evidence: Effort controls thinking depth and cost; thinking is billed as output tokens.

question: A team migrates a summarization pipeline to a newer Sonnet release whose tokenizer is different from the old one. Prompts and traffic are identical, yet invoices rise about 25% and some long summaries now end with stop_reason max_tokens. They need (1) an accurate cost forecast and (2) a fix for the truncation. (Select TWO.)

options.A: Scale the old token counts by a fixed ratio taken from a third-party tokenizer library's published benchmark
options.B: Estimate new costs by running existing prompts through the count_tokens endpoint with the new model ID
options.C: Assume cost per request is unchanged because the character count of every prompt stayed the same
options.D: Keep max_tokens and trim system prompts until the old token counts match the previous release
options.E: Raise max_tokens and re-check context budgets, since the same text can now map to more tokens

rationale: Different tokenizers produce different counts for the same text, so cost forecasts must come from the token counting endpoint for the exact model (B), and output and context budgets sized for the old tokenizer need headroom (E). (A) other tokenizers do not match Claude's. (D) trimming prompts changes behavior and does not fix output truncation. (C) character count does not determine token count.
evidence: Use POST /v1/messages/count_tokens, not other tokenizers; newer tokenizers can use more tokens, so re-baseline costs when migrating.

question: A publisher runs 300,000 article-summarization calls overnight on Sonnet. Results are needed by 7 a.m., no user waits on any single call, and the synchronous worker pool keeps hitting 429 rate-limit errors. Each article is unique, so no long prefix is shared between requests. Which change cuts cost and removes the rate-limit pressure?

options.A: Add a 1-hour cache breakpoint on each article so repeated retries of the same text are cheaper to run
options.B: Enable streaming on every call so the worker pool finishes each request faster and frees up capacity sooner
options.C: Submit the jobs through the Message Batches API and match each result to its article by custom_id
options.D: Move the entire job to the smallest tier and shrink the worker pool until 429 errors stop

rationale: The workload is asynchronous with a loose deadline, which is what the Batches API is for: lower per-token cost, no real-time rate-limit juggling, and results returned in any order so they are keyed by custom_id. (B) streaming changes delivery, not cost or throughput limits. (A) unique articles share no reusable prefix, so caching saves little. (D) changing tiers without an eval risks quality and does not need to be the first lever.
evidence: Message Batches API: asynchronous, 50% cost, results within 24h, results in any order so key by custom_id.

question: A customer-chat widget calls Sonnet without streaming and returns a full 700-token answer after about 6 seconds. Total generation time is acceptable to the business, but users complain the screen stays blank and they abandon the chat. An eval shows Haiku falls below the quality bar for this domain. What is the best change?

options.A: Move the traffic to the Batches API so the provider can schedule the work during off-peak hours of the day
options.B: Stream the response and render text deltas as they arrive, so users see the first words in well under a second
options.C: Lower max_tokens to 200 so the model is forced to stop producing text earlier than it otherwise would
options.D: Put a cache breakpoint on the user message so the model can skip reading it on every request

rationale: The complaint is perceived latency (time to first token), which streaming fixes directly without touching quality or tier. (A) batch is asynchronous and would make waiting worse. (C) truncating at 200 tokens cuts answers off mid-sentence. (D) the user message is volatile and cacheable prefixes do not address the blank screen.
evidence: Streaming improves time-to-first-token perceived latency, not total cost.

question: A due-diligence tool builds a report from five independent sections. It calls Claude once per section, one after another, and each call takes about 4 seconds, so the user waits 20 seconds against an 8-second budget. No section depends on another's output. Which change meets the budget without lowering the model tier?

options.A: Submit the five sections through the Batches API and poll until the results come back
options.B: Ask for all five sections in a single request so the model writes them in one longer response
options.C: Switch on streaming for each sequential call so every section appears while it is generated
options.D: Issue the five section requests concurrently, then assemble the results in order

rationale: Independent calls can run in parallel, so total latency drops toward the slowest single call (about 4 s). (B) one long response is generated sequentially and typically takes longer than any single section call. (C) streaming improves time to first token but the five calls still run back to back. (A) batches are asynchronous and can take far longer than 8 seconds.
evidence: Latency levers: parallel calls for independent work, streaming for time-to-first-token, smaller model, shorter output.

question:
A moderation endpoint labels short user comments as safe or unsafe, about 3 million per day, with a 3-second p95 budget. The current request is shown below, and the labels are single words. The team wants lower cost and latency while keeping quality measured on its labeled set.

```json
{
  "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
  "max_tokens": 16000,
  "thinking": {"type": "adaptive"},
  "output_config": {"effort": "max"},
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Label: ..."}]
}
```

Which change best fits?

options.A: Add a thinking budget_tokens value of 1024 so the model cannot reason longer than a short allowance
options.B: Lower effort to low and evaluate Haiku on the labeled set for this simple task
options.C: Keep effort at max and add streaming so the single-word label reaches the client sooner
options.D: Add temperature set to 0 so the model skips alternatives and returns the label faster

rationale: A one-word label at 3M/day is simple, high-volume work: max effort on the top tier buys nothing, and thinking is billed as output. Lowering effort and measuring a smaller tier on the labeled set is the right sequence. (A) budget_tokens is removed on current models and returns 400. (C) streaming barely helps a one-word answer and the cost stays. (D) sampling parameters now return 400 and never sped up generation.
evidence: Low effort for simple/high-volume tasks; budget_tokens is removed (400) on current models; pick the cheapest tier that meets the bar.

question: A research agent on a 1M-token context model runs for 60 turns. By turn 40 the prompt is about 600,000 tokens, mostly stale web-fetch results, each turn costs more than the last, and answers are drifting toward early, irrelevant material. The team wants to keep working on the same task. What should they do?

options.A: Raise max_tokens so the model has more room to answer despite the large prompt
options.B: Move the whole history into the system prompt so prompt caching covers all of it
options.C: Upgrade to the most expensive tier because a stronger model ignores irrelevant context
options.D: Clear stale tool results with context editing, or compact older turns, and keep the distilled findings

rationale: Context budgeting means pruning what no longer helps: context editing clears old tool results (and compaction summarizes old turns), which cuts per-turn cost and drift. (A) max_tokens limits output, not input. (C) a stronger tier still pays for every token and does not remove the bloat. (B) caching lowers the price of repeated tokens but leaves the bloat and drift in place.
evidence: Compaction summarizes old context server-side; context editing clears old tool results/thinking.

question:
After switching a JSON-extraction call to claude-sonnet-5-5, the service returns 400 errors. The API version in use rejects sampling parameters and does not accept an assistant message as the final turn. The call is:

```python
client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    temperature=0.2,
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": doc},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "{"},
    ],
)
```

Which TWO changes fix it while still getting valid JSON? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Swap temperature for top_p set to a similarly low value
options.B: Describe the schema in output_config.format and drop the prefill
options.C: Force the tool with tool_choice set to a specific tool name
options.D: Remove the temperature argument from the request
options.E: Add a stop sequence of a closing brace to emulate the prefill

rationale: Sampling parameters are rejected (D), and prefill is replaced by structured outputs through output_config.format, which gives schema-valid JSON without an assistant turn (B).
